IR.rationale: Bear steepening, with intermediate yields rising against the policy rate and the curve steepening, signals repricing of the expected path and term premium. Yield changes show short-horizon persistence, which carries into bond returns.

B.rationale: Widening credit spreads alongside weak high-yield returns mark a credit-stress state. This typically triggers flight-to-quality demand for Treasuries and lowers yields.

V.rationale: Elevated equity implied volatility reflects risk aversion and safe-haven demand for government bonds. That depresses yields and supports bond returns.

AP.rationale: Since the late 1990s the stock-bond correlation has been negative. Weak equity returns therefore coincide with, and briefly lead, falling yields.

ST.rationale: The equity style factors have no clear mechanism linking them to government bond returns beyond what the market factor already captures.

FX.rationale: Yen appreciation is a classic risk-off and carry-unwind signal that accompanies falling US yields.

COM.rationale: Broad commodity rallies raise inflation expectations and policy-rate expectations, which pressures nominal bond prices; inflation-linked bonds respond differently.

MC.rationale: Rising breakevens with no deterioration in jobless claims describe a reflationary state. In that state nominal yields tend to drift higher.

ENDG.rationale: Bond indices show time-series momentum at weekly to quarterly horizons, so strong recent returns tend to persist.

IR.rationale: A rising 1-year yield relative to fed funds signals repricing toward tightening. Policy-path uncertainty is a main driver of rate volatility.

B.rationale: Credit spread widening signals deteriorating risk appetite. That tends to bring large flight-to-quality swings in Treasury yields.

V.rationale: High equity volatility and high policy uncertainty together mark a broad uncertainty regime. In that regime interest-rate volatility (MOVE) rises along with risk-asset volatility.

AP.rationale: Equity sell-offs are followed by higher volatility across asset classes, a leverage and risk-aversion effect that spills into safe-haven bond flows.

ST.rationale: No documented mechanism links equity style factors to bond-market variance.

FX.rationale: Currency returns add little beyond the volatility and stress measures for forecasting bond variance.

COM.rationale: Commodity return shocks bear on breakevens but are weak, noisy predictors of aggregate bond variance.

MC.rationale: The St. Louis stress index includes bond-market implied volatility and funding spreads. High readings flag persistent turbulence in rates.

ENDG.rationale: Realised variance is persistent but mean-reverting. Unusually high recent variance indicates whether a volatility regime is in place beyond the baseline forecast.

IR.rationale: Bear steepening, with yields rising relative to policy and longer yields leading, is the typical precursor of sell-offs. These are driven by term premium and tantrum dynamics and produce tail losses in duration-heavy indices.

B.rationale: Strong risk-on credit conditions reduce safe-haven demand. Rotation out of Treasuries can then push yields sharply higher.

V.rationale: A low-volatility, risk-seeking environment lacks flight-to-quality support. Bond losses are then driven by growth and inflation repricing.

AP.rationale: Strong equity rallies reflect growth optimism and rotation out of bonds. Under the negative stock-bond correlation, this is associated with rising yields.

ST.rationale: Equity style factors carry no clear information about bond tail losses.

FX.rationale: A weakening yen accompanies risk-on positioning and widening US-Japan yield differentials. It tends to coincide with rising US yields.

COM.rationale: Commodity price surges feed inflation expectations and hawkish policy repricing, raising the odds of a sharp nominal bond sell-off.

MC.rationale: Rising breakeven inflation signals an inflation-risk repricing that pushes nominal yields up, the main source of large bond losses.

ENDG.rationale: Momentum in bond returns means that weak recent returns raise the probability of further large losses.

IR.rationale: Falling front-end and intermediate yields relative to fed funds mean the market is pricing easing or a growth scare. This is the state in which bond rallies extend.

B.rationale: Credit stress drives flight-to-quality flows into Treasuries, the main source of outsized bond gains.

V.rationale: Spikes in equity volatility coincide with safe-haven buying of government bonds and sharp yield declines.

AP.rationale: Equity sell-offs, under a negative stock-bond correlation, accompany large bond rallies.

ST.rationale: No clear mechanism links equity style factors to bond tail gains.

FX.rationale: Yen strength signals risk-off and carry unwinds, which typically coincide with strong Treasury rallies.

COM.rationale: Falling oil prices lower inflation expectations and signal weaker growth, supporting large declines in nominal yields.

MC.rationale: Elevated financial stress raises demand for safe, liquid government bonds and the likelihood of policy easing.

ENDG.rationale: Time-series momentum means strong recent bond returns raise the probability of further large gains.
